score_1_desc: No defined receiving process for inbound produce. Crates are unloaded and moved into the facility with no time stamping, no dock scheduling, and no ownership of the inward step.
score_2_desc: A basic receiving process exists but is manual and inconsistent - some inbound batches are logged on paper or a spreadsheet, others aren't tracked at all, and dock timing varies by whoever is on shift.
score_3_desc: A standardized dock SOP is documented and generally followed: inbound trucks are scheduled, crates are logged against a purchase order, and receiving time is recorded manually or in a basic tool.
score_4_desc: Receiving is actively managed against a dock-to-shelf time KPI, with system-logged timestamps, deviations flagged, and vendor punctuality tracked and reviewed.
score_5_desc: Dock scheduling and inbound logging are fully digitized and integrated with the WMS; dock-to-shelf time is continuously monitored and used to renegotiate vendor delivery windows.

score_1_desc: No formal grading of incoming produce. Acceptance/rejection is a subjective, ad-hoc call with no documented standard for ripeness, bruising, or size.
score_2_desc: A basic grading checklist exists for a few high-volume SKUs, but it's applied inconsistently and mostly from memory rather than a written spec.
score_3_desc: A standardized grading rubric (ripeness stage, blemish tolerance, size band) is documented per SKU category and used at the dock, with rejected batches logged.
score_4_desc: Grading is actively managed with photo-referenced standards, sampling-based inspection at defined intervals, and rejection-rate KPIs reviewed with vendors.
score_5_desc: Grading is best-in-class: digitized (e.g. handheld/photo-based grading capture), tied directly to vendor scorecards, and rejection data feeds back into sourcing decisions automatically.

score_1_desc: No batch or lot identification on inbound produce - once inside the facility, a crate's origin and receipt date can't be reliably traced.
score_2_desc: Batch/lot numbers are assigned manually with a marker or paper tag, but records aren't centrally kept and are frequently lost or illegible.
score_3_desc: A standardized batch-tagging process (vendor, receipt date, lot) is documented and applied consistently, with a manual or spreadsheet-based log kept.
score_4_desc: Batch/lot data is captured in a system at receiving and can be traced through storage and picking; discrepancies are investigated.
score_5_desc: Full lot-level traceability from dock to dispatch is system-enforced and barcode/QR-driven, enabling instant recall or root-cause tracing for any batch.

score_1_desc: No temperature monitoring in storage areas. Cooling is assumed to be working; there's no record of actual conditions produce is held at.
score_2_desc: Temperature is checked manually and irregularly (e.g. a wall thermometer glanced at occasionally), with no logging or escalation if out of range.
score_3_desc: A standardized temperature-check SOP exists with scheduled manual readings logged on paper or a spreadsheet, and a defined acceptable range per zone.
score_4_desc: Temperature is monitored with sensors and logged on a defined cadence; excursions trigger a documented escalation and corrective action process.
score_5_desc: Continuous automated temperature/humidity monitoring with real-time alerts, historical trend data, and integration into a cold-chain compliance dashboard.

score_1_desc: All produce is stored together regardless of temperature sensitivity or ethylene sensitivity, with no zoning at all.
score_2_desc: Some informal separation exists (e.g. "cold stuff over there") but it's not documented or consistently enforced across shifts.
score_3_desc: Storage zones are defined and labeled by temperature band and ethylene sensitivity, with a documented placement guide for common SKUs.
score_4_desc: Zone assignment is actively enforced through put-away rules and periodically audited; misplacement is tracked and corrected.
score_5_desc: Zoning is system-enforced at put-away (WMS blocks incorrect placement), with zone-level condition monitoring tied to individual SKU shelf-life outcomes.

score_1_desc: No humidity or airflow management - produce is stored in whatever ambient conditions the facility happens to have.
score_2_desc: Basic ventilation (fans, open doors) is used opportunistically but there's no target humidity range or consistent practice.
score_3_desc: A documented humidity/ventilation standard exists per storage zone, with equipment (humidifiers, exhaust) assigned and checked periodically.
score_4_desc: Humidity is actively monitored against targets with corrective actions logged when out of range, and equipment maintenance is scheduled.
score_5_desc: Humidity and airflow are automatically controlled and logged per zone, tuned per produce category, and reviewed against spoilage outcomes to refine targets.

score_1_desc: No defined slotting logic - produce is placed wherever there's open space, with no regard to velocity, shelf-life, or picker travel distance.
score_2_desc: Slotting follows informal habits of experienced staff, but it's not documented and breaks down when they're not on shift.
score_3_desc: A documented slotting plan exists based on velocity and shelf-life (fast-moving, short-life SKUs near pack-out), generally followed.
score_4_desc: Slotting is actively reviewed against sales velocity data and adjusted on a defined cadence; deviations from plan are tracked.
score_5_desc: Slotting is dynamically optimized (system-recommended or algorithm-driven) based on real-time velocity, shelf-life, and pick-path efficiency.

score_1_desc: No put-away time expectation or process - produce can sit at the dock for an unpredictable amount of time before being shelved.
score_2_desc: A rough put-away expectation exists informally but isn't tracked, and delays are common during peak inbound periods.
score_3_desc: A documented put-away SOP with a target time-to-shelf exists and is generally followed under normal conditions.
score_4_desc: Put-away time is actively measured against the KPI, with staffing adjusted for peak inbound volume and delays investigated.
score_5_desc: Put-away is system-directed (task assignment, guided locations) and time-to-shelf is a continuously tracked, best-in-class-benchmarked metric.

score_1_desc: No first-expiry-first-out discipline - older stock and newer stock are picked interchangeably, with no visibility into which is which.
score_2_desc: FEFO is understood informally by experienced pickers but isn't enforced by any process or system, and is frequently skipped under time pressure.
score_3_desc: A documented FEFO process exists (e.g. date-labeled bins, front-to-back stocking) and is generally followed with periodic spot checks.
score_4_desc: FEFO adherence is actively audited on a defined schedule, with violations tracked and corrective coaching given.
score_5_desc: FEFO is system-enforced at pick (the WMS directs pickers to the oldest eligible batch), with adherence continuously measured near 100%.

score_1_desc: No shelf-life tracking at all - there's no way to know how close any given batch is to becoming unsellable until it visibly spoils.
score_2_desc: Shelf-life is estimated informally by appearance/smell rather than tracked from receipt date, and is inconsistent across staff.
score_3_desc: A documented shelf-life standard per SKU (days from receipt) is defined and used to flag aging stock manually.
score_4_desc: Remaining shelf-life is actively tracked per batch, with aging stock flagged for markdown or priority picking on a defined cadence.
score_5_desc: Shelf-life is tracked per batch in a system that automatically flags at-risk inventory and triggers markdown, redistribution, or priority-pick workflows.

score_1_desc: No cycle counting - system/paper stock levels and physical stock are not reconciled, and discrepancies are only discovered when a pick fails.
score_2_desc: Counts happen occasionally and informally, with no defined frequency or accuracy target.
score_3_desc: A documented cycle-count schedule exists (e.g. weekly per zone) with a defined accuracy target, and discrepancies are logged.
score_4_desc: Cycle counts are actively tracked against an accuracy KPI, with root causes of variance investigated and corrected.
score_5_desc: Cycle counting is continuous/perpetual (not just periodic), system-driven, with accuracy consistently above a best-in-class threshold and variance trends analyzed.

score_1_desc: Replenishment to dark stores/fulfillment points is reactive and ad-hoc - triggered only after a stockout is noticed.
score_2_desc: A rough replenishment schedule exists but is manually decided each time with no consistent trigger logic.
score_3_desc: A documented replenishment cadence and trigger threshold (e.g. par level) exists per SKU category and is generally followed.
score_4_desc: Replenishment triggers are actively tuned against sell-through data and adjusted for known demand spikes (e.g. weekends, promotions).
score_5_desc: Replenishment is dynamically automated based on real-time sell-through, shelf-life, and demand signals, minimizing both stockouts and over-replenishment of perishables.

score_1_desc: No forecasting - order quantities are guessed or based on whatever was ordered last time, with no reference to actual demand.
score_2_desc: A basic forecast exists (e.g. last week's sales) but doesn't account for perishability, seasonality, or promotions.
score_3_desc: A documented forecasting method incorporating recent sales trends and shelf-life constraints is used and generally followed.
score_4_desc: Forecasts are actively reviewed against actuals on a defined cadence, with accuracy tracked and adjustments made for known demand drivers.
score_5_desc: Forecasting is system/model-driven, incorporating seasonality, promotions, and shelf-life risk, with continuous accuracy monitoring and feedback loops.

score_1_desc: Stockouts and overstock (leading to spoilage) both happen frequently with no tracking of either, and no attempt to balance the two.
score_2_desc: Stockouts and overstock are noticed anecdotally but not measured, so it's unclear which SKUs or stores are worst affected.
score_3_desc: Stockout rate and overstock/spoilage-linked-to-overstock are documented and tracked at a basic level per SKU category.
score_4_desc: Both metrics are actively monitored against targets, with root causes reviewed and replenishment parameters adjusted accordingly.
score_5_desc: Stockout and overstock are jointly optimized in a single system view, with SKU-level parameters continuously tuned to minimize both simultaneously.

score_1_desc: No defined process for picking loose or weight-based produce (e.g. picked by eye, no weighing step, no accuracy check).
score_2_desc: A basic weighing step exists for some SKUs but isn't consistently applied or checked, leading to frequent under/over-fulfillment.
score_3_desc: A documented pick-and-weigh SOP with a tolerance band exists per SKU and is generally followed.
score_4_desc: Pick accuracy for weighted SKUs is actively measured against a tolerance KPI, with deviations tracked back to individual pickers for coaching.
score_5_desc: Pick-and-weigh is system-verified at the point of pack (integrated scale, automatic flag on out-of-tolerance), with accuracy consistently best-in-class.

score_1_desc: No standard for how produce is packed for delivery - packaging choice is left entirely to whoever is packing, with frequent transit damage.
score_2_desc: A basic packaging guideline exists for a few fragile SKUs but isn't documented or consistently applied.
score_3_desc: A documented packaging standard per produce category (crush-resistance, ventilation, ice packs where needed) exists and is generally followed.
score_4_desc: Transit-damage rates are actively tracked back to packaging choices, with the standard updated based on damage data.
score_5_desc: Packaging is continuously optimized per SKU based on transit-damage analytics, with near-zero damage-related returns/complaints.

score_1_desc: Spoilage is not tracked at all - unsellable produce is simply discarded with no record of quantity, SKU, or cause.
score_2_desc: Spoilage is estimated informally (e.g. "a lot this week") but not logged with any consistency or granularity.
score_3_desc: A documented process for logging spoiled/discarded produce (SKU, quantity, reason) exists and is generally followed.
score_4_desc: Spoilage is actively tracked as a % of throughput per SKU, reviewed on a defined cadence, and compared against a target.
score_5_desc: Spoilage is tracked in real time per SKU/batch with automated reporting, benchmarked against a best-in-class shrinkage target, and directly feeds sourcing/replenishment decisions.

score_1_desc: No investigation into why produce spoils - it's treated as an unavoidable cost of doing business rather than a solvable problem.
score_2_desc: Causes are occasionally guessed at informally, but no structured analysis or corrective action is taken.
score_3_desc: A documented process exists to categorize spoilage causes (over-order, cold-chain break, aged stock, damage) and review them periodically.
score_4_desc: Root causes are actively analyzed against the tracked spoilage data, with corrective actions assigned and their impact monitored.
score_5_desc: Root-cause analysis is continuous and data-driven, with corrective actions automatically prioritized by impact and their effectiveness tracked over time.

score_1_desc: No formal write-off process - spoiled stock disappears from the floor with no reconciliation against inventory records.
score_2_desc: Write-offs are recorded manually and inconsistently, often after the fact and without approval or verification.
score_3_desc: A documented write-off SOP (verification, approval, disposal method, inventory reconciliation) exists and is generally followed.
score_4_desc: Write-offs are actively reconciled against inventory on a defined cadence, with unusual patterns flagged for review.
score_5_desc: Write-off and disposal are system-integrated with inventory (automatic reconciliation), fully auditable, and disposal method is optimized (e.g. donation/composting where viable) to reduce cost and waste impact.

score_1_desc: No defined process at collection centers - produce is aggregated from farmers/vendors with no receiving discipline or condition checks before onward transit.
score_2_desc: A basic CC receiving practice exists informally but varies by center and staff, with minimal documentation.
score_3_desc: A documented CC receiving and staging SOP exists and is generally followed across centers.
score_4_desc: CC handling is actively monitored against the SOP, with condition-at-CC data tracked and deviations corrected.
score_5_desc: CC operations are standardized and digitally monitored across all centers, with condition data feeding directly into downstream quality decisions.

score_1_desc: No vendor performance management - vendors are engaged transactionally with no tracked history or scorecard.
score_2_desc: Vendor performance is known informally by procurement staff but isn't documented or shared with vendors.
score_3_desc: A documented vendor scorecard exists and is generally used to inform sourcing decisions.
score_4_desc: Vendor scorecards are actively reviewed on a defined cadence, with underperforming vendors coached or phased out.
score_5_desc: Vendor performance is continuously tracked and automatically informs sourcing allocation, with scorecards shared transparently with vendors.

score_1_desc: No deliberate flow design - inbound, storage, and outbound zones overlap with no defined traffic pattern, causing constant congestion.
score_2_desc: A rough flow pattern exists informally based on how the facility happened to be set up, not deliberately designed.
score_3_desc: A documented flow pattern (U-shaped, criss-cross, or straight-through) is defined and the layout generally follows it.
score_4_desc: Flow effectiveness is actively measured (travel distance, congestion points) and the layout is adjusted based on findings.
score_5_desc: Flow design is continuously optimized using real movement data, with layout changes data-justified rather than assumed.

score_1_desc: No slot scheduling exists for docks - trucks and activities compete for space with no allocation logic.
score_2_desc: A rough informal allocation exists based on whoever arrives first, not planned in advance.
score_3_desc: A documented dock/slot allocation plan exists and is generally followed.
score_4_desc: Slot allocation is actively reviewed against utilization data and adjusted to reduce idle/conflict time.
score_5_desc: Slot scheduling is dynamically optimized (system-assisted) based on real-time inbound/outbound demand.

score_1_desc: Rejected produce has no defined handling - it sits mixed with accepted stock or is disposed of inconsistently with no record.
score_2_desc: Rejected goods are set aside informally but the next step (return, dispose, downgrade) isn't standardized.
score_3_desc: A documented disposition process for rejected goods exists and is generally followed.
score_4_desc: Disposition decisions are actively tracked and reviewed for consistency and cost impact.
score_5_desc: Disposition is systematized with clear rules per rejection reason, fully auditable and cost-tracked.

score_1_desc: Rejection reasons are never communicated back to vendors - the same quality issues recur shipment after shipment.
score_2_desc: Feedback happens informally and inconsistently, often only when a vendor asks.
score_3_desc: A documented process communicates rejection reasons to vendors and is generally followed.
score_4_desc: Rejection trends are actively analyzed and shared with vendors on a defined cadence to drive improvement.
score_5_desc: Rejection feedback is automatic and data-rich, directly linked to the vendor scorecard and sourcing decisions.

score_1_desc: No defined process for handling returns - returned goods are handled ad hoc with no consistent intake or disposition.
score_2_desc: A rough informal return-handling practice exists but isn't documented or consistent.
score_3_desc: A documented return intake and processing SOP exists and is generally followed.
score_4_desc: Return processing is actively measured (time-to-disposition) and reviewed for efficiency.
score_5_desc: Return processing is system-tracked end to end, with disposition decisions automated where possible.

score_1_desc: Return reasons are never analyzed - returns are treated as an unavoidable cost with no attempt to reduce them.
score_2_desc: Reasons are occasionally noted informally but not compiled or acted on.
score_3_desc: A documented process tracks return reasons and reviews them on a basic level.
score_4_desc: Return root causes are actively analyzed and fed back into upstream process changes (packaging, picking accuracy).
score_5_desc: Return prevention is data-driven and continuous, with root-cause patterns automatically routed to the responsible process owner.

score_1_desc: Customer complaints aren't captured in any structured way - they're handled verbally and forgotten.
score_2_desc: Complaints are logged informally and inconsistently, often without enough detail to trace back to a cause.
score_3_desc: A documented complaint-logging process exists and is generally followed, with basic detail captured.
score_4_desc: Complaint logging is actively audited for completeness, and complaints are traceable back to a batch/vendor where relevant.
score_5_desc: Complaint capture is systematic and fully traceable to source batch/vendor, feeding automatically into quality dashboards.

score_1_desc: Complaints have no defined resolution process - some get addressed, most don't, with no tracking either way.
score_2_desc: Resolution happens informally and inconsistently, with no ownership or time expectation.
score_3_desc: A documented resolution process (ownership, time target) exists and is generally followed.
score_4_desc: Resolution time and outcomes are actively tracked against targets, with overdue complaints escalated.
score_5_desc: Resolution is systematically tracked end to end, with resolution-time and root-cause data feeding continuous improvement.

score_1_desc: No documented policy exists for how operations should run, and nothing is monitored on any regular cadence.
score_2_desc: Policies exist informally in people's heads; monitoring happens sporadically when someone thinks to check.
score_3_desc: Documented policies exist and a monitoring cadence (daily/weekly) is defined and generally followed.
score_4_desc: Monitoring cadence is actively adhered to and reviewed, with policy updated based on findings.
score_5_desc: Policy and monitoring are continuously maintained, with real-time dashboards replacing manual checks.

score_1_desc: No thresholds or escalation triggers are defined - problems are noticed only when they become severe enough to be obvious.
score_2_desc: Informal thresholds exist in some people's judgment but aren't documented or consistently applied.
score_3_desc: Documented thresholds and an escalation path exist and are generally followed.
score_4_desc: Threshold breaches are actively tracked, with escalation response time measured.
score_5_desc: Thresholds are system-monitored with automatic real-time escalation and tracked resolution.

score_1_desc: No market intelligence is gathered at all - sourcing and pricing decisions are made blind to what's happening in the market.
score_2_desc: Market information is picked up informally and inconsistently by individual buyers.
score_3_desc: A documented process for daily market intelligence gathering exists and is generally followed.
score_4_desc: Market intelligence is actively used to inform sourcing/pricing decisions and reviewed for accuracy.
score_5_desc: Market intelligence is systematically captured and directly feeds forecasting and sourcing decisions in near real time.

score_1_desc: No benchmarking against other players or defined norms exists - performance is judged with no external or internal reference point.
score_2_desc: Benchmarking happens informally and occasionally, not systematically tracked.
score_3_desc: A documented benchmarking process (benchmark companies, hub-wise norms) exists and is generally referenced.
score_4_desc: Benchmarks are actively reviewed and updated, with performance measured against them regularly.
score_5_desc: Benchmarking is continuous and systematically maintained, directly informing target-setting across the business.

score_1_desc: No training program exists - new staff learn entirely on the job from whoever happens to be nearby.
score_2_desc: Informal training happens (shadowing an experienced colleague) but there's no defined curriculum.
score_3_desc: A documented training curriculum exists per role and is generally used.
score_4_desc: The curriculum is actively reviewed and updated to reflect current SOPs.
score_5_desc: Training design is continuously refined based on performance data and directly linked to every current SOP.

score_1_desc: Training delivery isn't tracked at all - there's no record of who was trained on what, or whether it worked.
score_2_desc: Training happens informally with no completion record or effectiveness check.
score_3_desc: A documented process tracks training completion and is generally followed.
score_4_desc: Training completion is actively tracked against targets, with effectiveness spot-checked.
score_5_desc: Training completion and effectiveness are systematically tracked, with competency verified before staff work unsupervised.

score_1_desc: Staffing levels are never planned against volume - headcount is whatever it happens to be, causing chronic under- or overstaffing.
score_2_desc: Staffing is adjusted informally and reactively when problems become visible.
score_3_desc: A documented staffing plan tied to volume/activity exists and is generally followed.
score_4_desc: Staffing adequacy is actively reviewed against actual volume and adjusted proactively.
score_5_desc: Staffing is dynamically planned using volume forecasts, with adequacy continuously monitored and adjusted.

score_1_desc: Roles and responsibilities aren't defined - staff figure out what to do based on whatever's in front of them each day.
score_2_desc: Roles exist informally but overlap and gaps are common, with no documentation.
score_3_desc: Documented role/responsibility definitions exist and are generally followed.
score_4_desc: Role clarity is actively reinforced through review, and attrition is tracked with basic follow-up.
score_5_desc: Roles are clearly defined, continuously reinforced, and attrition is proactively managed with root-cause analysis.

score_1_desc: No KPIs are defined for operations at all - success or failure is judged subjectively, if at all.
score_2_desc: Some informal notion of what matters exists but isn't written down as defined metrics.
score_3_desc: Documented KPIs exist for key operational areas and are generally referenced.
score_4_desc: KPIs are actively reviewed for relevance and ownership is assigned to each one.
score_5_desc: KPIs are comprehensively defined, owned, and reviewed on a regular cadence for continued relevance.

score_1_desc: Even where KPIs are defined, they're never actually tracked - there's no dashboard, report, or regular view of performance.
score_2_desc: Tracking happens informally and inconsistently, often via ad hoc spreadsheets that go stale.
score_3_desc: A documented tracking/dashboarding process exists and is generally maintained and reviewed.
score_4_desc: Dashboards are actively used to drive decisions, with refresh cadence and data quality actively monitored.
score_5_desc: Dashboards are real-time, comprehensive, and demonstrably drive day-to-day decision-making.

score_1_desc: No cost tracking exists at the operational level - costs are known only at a high, aggregated financial-statement level, if at all.
score_2_desc: Some cost awareness exists informally ("labor is expensive") without actual tracked figures.
score_3_desc: A documented cost-tracking process (cost-per-unit, per-order, or similar) exists and is generally maintained.
score_4_desc: Cost tracking is actively reviewed against targets/benchmarks and used to inform operational decisions.
score_5_desc: Cost tracking is granular, real-time, and directly drives operational decision-making across the business.

score_1_desc: The cost of quality failures (spoilage, rejections, complaints) is invisible - it's absorbed as a general loss with no specific number attached.
score_2_desc: The cost is estimated roughly and informally without a consistent calculation method.
score_3_desc: A documented process quantifies the cost of quality failures on a basic level.
score_4_desc: Cost-of-quality-failure is actively tracked as a KPI and reviewed with stakeholders.
score_5_desc: Cost-of-quality-failure is tracked in real time and directly reported to stakeholders to prioritize corrective investment.
